evaluation.positioning_hook: A bored commuter discovers his exact double’s grave, then quietly remakes himself into the dead man before following a stranger home with violent intent.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean psychological-thriller engine, but the script’s appeal is narrow and heavily dependent on taste for ambiguity and menace. The final turn into domestic violence and stalking gives it a hard edge, but there isn’t yet a broad emotional or commercial promise beyond the central unease.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook is easy to state: Frank sees a grave with his own name and face, then begins to inhabit that dead man’s identity. The script lands that premise clearly by the grave reveal and the newspaper article in scenes 12 and 18, though the larger dramatic question remains more atmospheric than fully engineered.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Frank is specific in his boredom and eventual sinister turn, but he is not yet especially layered on the page; his wife and daughter are present more as domestic context than as fully dimensional counterweights. The role could attract an actor looking for a controlled descent, but the character’s inner life is mostly implied rather than dramatized.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The dead-man identity premise is unusual and memorable, and the moustache detail gives the script a strange, almost ritualistic specificity. That said, the execution is very spare and the boldness comes more from the premise than from a fully distinctive dramatic approach.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script is built from repeated commuting and office beats, which creates a deliberate monotony but also limits escalation until the late attack. The central turn arrives relatively late, and after the assault the script ends quickly, so the momentum is more mood-based than propulsive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a man becoming the dead man he found in a grave is fresh and immediately legible, especially with the visual echo of the moustache and the family photo. What keeps it from scoring higher is that the script stops just as the premise becomes most unsettling, so the resonance is strong but not yet fully explored.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is intentionally minimal: train platform, train carriage, office, cemetery, home. That restraint supports the concept, but there is little social texture or system-level detail beyond Frank’s routine, so the setting functions more as a container than a world with its own story-generating rules.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistently cold, repetitive, and quietly sinister, with the commuter routine becoming a kind of ritual. It has a clear mood, but the script is so stripped down that the tonal identity is more austere than singular.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper psychological material in the grave, the family photo, and Frank’s shift into a new identity, but the script does not yet open those layers on the page. A buyer can sense a larger interior story, though most of it remains offscreen.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is essentially a solo-protagonist piece with functional supporting presence from wife, daughter, and the stranger on the train. The relationships do not generate recurring dramatic engine; they mainly serve as context for Frank’s internal drift.

lead_characters.name: Frank
lead_characters.demographics: Male, middle-aged, married, office worker; contemporary working-class or lower-middle-class commuter.
lead_characters.hook: Frank is a dead-eyed commuter whose life is defined by routine until he finds a grave bearing his own name and an exact visual double. He starts as a bored, detached husband and father, then quietly hardens into someone capable of stalking and brutal violence; the moustache becomes a small but chilling marker of self-invention.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Jake Gyllenhaal in Nightcrawler — a controlled, inward performance that slowly tips into menace. It gives an actor the chance to play stillness, obsession, and a late-breaking moral collapse without ever leaving the frame.

lead_characters.name: Wife
lead_characters.hook: Frank’s wife is the domestic anchor of the script, appearing in brief home and phone scenes that underline how little of his inner life she can access. She functions as the normal world he is drifting away from, and the family photo gives her a quiet emotional weight even without much dialogue.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained, emotionally precise supporting role that gave Laura Linney in The Savages or Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April room to make a few scenes register hard. It offers an actor the chance to build a whole relationship through subtext and reaction.

lead_characters.name: Daughter
lead_characters.demographics: Female, child or young teen, Frank’s daughter.
lead_characters.hook: Frank’s daughter is part of the family tableau that keeps reminding us what he stands to lose or destroy. She is not written as a character with a separate arc, but she sharpens the unease around his emotional vacancy at home.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but meaningful child role in the vein of the daughter parts in Manchester by the Sea or Room — less about speeches, more about being the emotional barometer in a fractured home. It gives a young actor a chance to play ordinary family life against a growing dread.

lead_characters.name: Man on train
lead_characters.hook: The stranger on the train is the trigger for Frank’s final violent act, a blank presence who becomes the object of Frank’s fixation. He is less a character than a pressure point, but he is essential to the script’s last movement.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can be played with minimal dialogue but strong physical presence, similar to the anonymous targets in Drive or The Guest. For a character actor, it is a clean, memorable function in a tense sequence.

casting_characteristics: lookalike/doppelganger implication for the grave photo and newspaper image

technical.vfx_details: No visible effects requirements; the grave photo and newspaper image can be handled practically or with simple graphic design.
technical.sfx_needs: One brief assault sequence and basic newspaper/phone props.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical, streamer original, or festival-to-streaming path.

budget.note: Contemporary, five core locations, no VFX, and only one brief assault sequence — this stays comfortably contained if the train and cemetery are scoped efficiently.

casting.note: The lead needs an actor who can play deadened routine, quiet obsession, and sudden violence without broadening the material. The child role is small, but the whole piece still lives or dies on the lead’s face.

development.note: The concept is clear, but the script is extremely spare, so buyers will weigh whether the grave reveal and final attack are enough dramatic architecture for a feature. The domestic thread with the wife and daughter is present, but only lightly dramatized.

comp_set.title: The Machinist
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the same psychological erosion, working-man alienation, and bleak visual minimalism, with a lead performance built around physical and mental drift.

comp_set.title: Take Shelter
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it turns ordinary domestic life into a slow-burn descent where the audience is asked to track a man’s private unraveling.

comp_set.title: Enemy
comp_set.why_it_comps: The doppelganger-adjacent identity disturbance and uncanny visual repetition make this a close tonal and conceptual cousin.

comp_set.title: The Invitation
comp_set.why_it_comps: It uses a restrained, low-budget thriller frame to build dread from social normalcy before a late violent turn.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like psychological thrillers with a bleak, art-house edge and a strong central performance.
audience_target.demographics: 35-54 skew, slightly male-leaning but viable for adult genre audiences across genders, especially viewers who favor festival-thriller and prestige-indie titles.

budget_tier.note: A small cast, contemporary settings, and no effects keep this in the low indie range; the train access and assault scene are the main scope items.

types_of_buyers: producer-directors looking for a contained actor showcase
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of austere, actor-driven thrillers where mood and performance do the heavy lifting. It is especially attractive to buyers who want a contained concept with a clear hook and a low-cost path to a distinctive lead role.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with no clear sequel, prequel, or spinoff vector; the premise resolves around Frank’s private descent.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The grave reveal is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: That single image gives the project a clean marketing hook and a memorable trailer beat. It is the kind of premise that can get a buyer to understand the movie in one sentence and an actor to see a showcase role immediately.
strengths.evidence: Frank types the name from the grave into the computer and finds the newspaper article about the dead man who looks exactly like him.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The commuter routine creates a strong ritual frame.
strengths.what_it_means: The repeated train-platform-office-cemetery pattern gives the film a built-in visual grammar and a low-cost way to build dread. That kind of repetition is attractive to buyers looking for contained thrillers with a distinct formal identity.
strengths.evidence: Scenes 1 through 17 repeatedly cycle Frank through the same commute, office, and cemetery beats before the turn.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Frank is a clean descent role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead offers a contained, performance-forward arc that can anchor the whole package around one actor. Buyers and directors chasing prestige-genre material will recognize the value of a role that moves from blank routine to sinister intent.
strengths.evidence: Frank goes from staring into space at work to growing the moustache, following the man, and smiling after the attack.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The budget footprint is highly controllable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script can be made without heavy effects, large cast days, or expensive set pieces, which lowers the barrier to entry for indie financiers and streamer buyers. That makes it easier to package around concept and performance rather than scale.
strengths.evidence: The story lives in a train platform, train carriage, office, cemetery, and home, with one brief assault sequence.

whats_special.headline: This is a lean, actor-driven psychological thriller with a genuinely memorable central image: a commuter finds his own grave and starts becoming the dead man. The contained locations and minimal production demands make it an efficient buy for a buyer looking for prestige-genre material that can be sold on premise and performance.

items.area: The feature is built on a very thin dramatic spine.
items.detail: Most of the script is repetition of commute, office, and cemetery beats, with the core reveal landing late and the ending arriving almost immediately after the assault. That makes the buying conversation hinge on whether the premise alone is enough architecture for a full feature, which is a real development question rather than a polish note.

items.area: Frank’s interior life stays mostly implicit.
items.detail: We see boredom, fixation, and then violence, but very little of the psychological mechanism that connects those states. For a buyer, that means the lead role is attractive as a showcase but still somewhat opaque as a fully dimensional character engine.

items.area: The wife and daughter are functional, not generative.
items.detail: The domestic scenes establish stakes, but they do not create a strong relationship engine or a counterpoint that materially complicates Frank’s drift. That keeps the emotional field narrow and limits the ensemble value of the package.

items.area: The ending stops at the moment of escalation.
items.detail: Frank’s final entry into the house is a strong button, but it also means the script ends just as the premise becomes most volatile. Buyers will notice that the piece is more of a provocation than a fully paid-off narrative arc.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural: the concept is memorable, but the script is extremely spare and ends right as the psychological and domestic stakes should be peaking. That makes it a strong premise buy, but one that will invite questions about feature-length dramatic weight and character depth.
